quotes.quote: we introduce the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark, which transforms 304 diagnostically challenging New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference (NEJM-CPC) cases into stepwise diagnostic encounters
Performance is assessed not just by diagnostic accuracy but also by the cost of physician visits and tests performed
most evaluations of language models rely on static vignettes and multiple-choice questions that fail to reflect the complexity and nuance of evidence-based medicine in real-world settings
The Gatekeeper discloses specific clinical findings only when explicitly queried, and can synthesize additional case-consistent information for tests not described in the original CPC narrative
We set a cut-off of ≥ 4 on a five-point Likert scale to count as a “correct” diagnosis, based on the clinical rationale that clinical management would remain largely unchanged above this threshold
We implemented the Gatekeeper using a language model (o4-mini) with access to the full NEJM CPC case file, including the final diagnosis

Diagnostic test costs were determined using a language model-based lookup system designed to translate diagnostic test requests, provided in free-text format, into standardized Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes
We treat sequential patient-facing questions and physical examination findings as part of a standard physician visit, assigning a fixed cost of $300 per visit
These CPT codes were then matched to corresponding cost data derived from a 2023 pricing table published by a large U.S. health system, sourced under the CMS HHS price transparency rule (45 CFR §180)
Reviewers flagged only eight responses as potentially problematic, and none were judged to have leaked the diagnosis after group adjudication
After binarizing both the physician and Judge scores, we found that inter-rater agreement was strong - Cohen’s κ = 0.70 for the MAI-Dx set and κ = 0.87 for the human set
We collected 304 consecutive cases published between 2017 and 2025, converting each into an interactive simulation of sequential diagnostic reasoning
we changed the Gatekeeper to return realistic synthetic findings for queries not covered in the original text
The most recent 56 cases (from 2024–2025) were held out as a hidden test set to assess generalization performance
To establish human performance, we recruited 21 physicians practicing in the US or UK to act as diagnostic agents
Participants had a median of 12 years [IQR 6-24 years] of experience: 17 were primary care physicians and four were in-hospital generalists
Physicians were explicitly instructed not to use external resources, including search engines
Their average diagnostic accuracy was 19.9%
requesting 6.6 questions and 7.2 tests, resulting in an average cost of $2,963
it achieved 81.9% accuracy (vs off-the-shelf o3 at 78.6%) while reducing average test costs to $4,735 (from $7,850)
Notably, one configuration achieves 79.9% accuracy at the low cost of $2,396
we were able to improve accuracy to 85.5% with ensembling techniques, while still keeping the costs at $7,184 (from o3’s $7,850)
GPT-4o achieved 49.3% accuracy at a lower cost ($2,745 per case)
Even the physician performing at the highest diagnostic accuracy (41%) was outperformed by GPT-4o in both accuracy and cost
Each physician completed an average of 36 cases, providing a total of 764 human diagnoses over the 56 cases in the test set
MAI-DxO, establishes a new Pareto frontier that outperforms off-the-shelf models and physicians at every cost or accuracy level
there are no cases where the patients are in fact healthy or have benign syndromes
gains on hard cases generalize to common, everyday clinical conditions, and could not measure false positive rates
our medical cost estimates are best viewed as first-order approximations
we opted to recruit medical generalists only (primary care physicians and internal physicians)

We explored the capabilities of frontier language models in sequential diagnosis, a diagnostic paradigm that captures the iterative nature of clinical reasoning
Given a brief clinical presentation, clinicians selectively acquired information to reach a diagnosis, enabling assessment of diagnostic accuracy and workup cost

We developed an interactive benchmark and an artificial intelligence (AI) system that simulates a panel of physicians, continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests

the system achieved 83.2% accuracy on … clinicopathological conference cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED emergency department admissions, outperforming generalist physicians (36.1 and 46.8%, respectively)
Although these findings were obtained in a controlled benchmark setting, they highlight the promise of language models for supporting more accurate, lower-cost diagnoses

we created interactive case challenges drawn from the NEJM case series – what we call the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark (SD Bench)
This benchmark transforms 304 recent NEJM cases into stepwise diagnostic encounters where models – or human physicians – can iteratively ask questions and order tests
The best performing setup was MAI-DxO paired with OpenAI’s o3, which correctly solved 85.5% of the NEJM benchmark cases
we also evaluated 21 practicing physicians from the US and UK, each with 5-20 years of clinical experience
On the same tasks, these experts achieved a mean accuracy of 20% across completed cases
SD Bench and MAI-DxO are research demonstrations only and are not currently available as public benchmarks or orchestrators
The gatekeeper (gatekeeper.py) answers each test order / question from the case's full text, returning the real result when the case contains it or a synthetic result when it does not
When the agent commits a diagnosis, the judge (judge.py) scores it against the ground-truth diagnosis on a 1–5 Likert scale (4–5 counts as a correct diagnosis)
SDBench ships with a small, fully-synthetic dataset named synthetic (five NEJM-style CPC cases), which is the default dataset so the harness runs out of the box with no data access required
it should not be used to report diagnostic performance — use a clinically sourced dataset for that
The mimic dataset is distributed as MIMIC-IV-Ext-SDBench v1.0.0 on PhysioNet
Named configs in config.py pin the gatekeeper/judge models and prompt versions
We found the gpt-5-mini estimates to be 40-50% higher than the grounded estimates used in our paper
A typical grounding rate of 98%+ is expected, if the rate is significantly below that then your grounded cost results may be unreliable
In the published paper we reported on costs that were grounded against a public hospital charge master
By default it runs the baseline agent on the bundled synthetic train set (five cases) with GPT-5 using OpenRouter

Each case is scored on both diagnostic accuracy and the cost of the tests ordered, surfacing the accuracy–cost trade-offs that matter in practice
The system under test. Receives a short case summary that does not reveal the diagnosis and decides, turn by turn, to order tests, ask questions, or commit a diagnosis
Five fully-synthetic NEJM-style cases, included in the repository as the default dataset for open, access-free evaluation

MIMIC-IV-Ext-SDBench contains 488 case records derived from MIMIC-IV emergency department encounters in which the patient was subsequently admitted as an inpatient
The dataset is split into 163 train, 254 validation and 71 clinician-reviewed test cases

Each case is formatted primarily for use with the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark, an interactive diagnostic-reasoning benchmark in which an agent starts from a brief vignette and must request further information iteratively from a gatekeeper agent that mediates access to the underlying case record
Most diagnostic-AI evaluations rely on static vignettes that present all relevant findings upfront

By compressing diagnosis into one inference step, static benchmarks cannot measure whether a system asks the right questions, avoids indiscriminate testing, updates the differential diagnosis as evidence accrues, or recognizes when to conclude the workup
The Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark (SDBench) reframes diagnosis as an iterative encounter that scores both diagnostic accuracy and the cost of the workup

This dataset provides a selected cohort of routine emergency-department admissions that can be used for an SDBench evaluation, complementing the educational NEJM clinicopathological cases already used in SDBench with cases drawn from routine hospital documentation
ED-originated admissions are sampled, excluding direct-to-ICU admissions and limiting each patient to a single note
A brief, diagnosis-free initial vignette that includes the patient's de-id age and recorded sex is synthesised
All cases in the test split were then manually reviewed by clinicians for inclusion and for correctness of the ground-truth diagnosis. 13 ground-truth diagnoses were corrected during clinician review
Claude Opus 4.1 was used for steps 3 and 6, and GPT-5 mini for steps 4 and 5
Cases were screened for inclusion to ensure they have a clear presenting complaint, key clinical findings, and a definitive final diagnosis

When running SDBench with GPT-5, the baseline agent achieved 76.6% diagnostic accuracy on the 325 MIMIC-IV validation and test cases, while the Diagnostic Orchestrator (DxO) agent without budget constraints achieved 80.3%
Mean estimated workup costs were approximately US$4,240 and US$4,980 per case, respectively
test (71 cases): Clinician reviewed. Included in published SDBench evaluations as fully held-out data
The dataset contains selected hospital admissions with diagnosed conditions, so its case mix and disease prevalence do not represent all emergency presentations
The benchmark assesses diagnostic correctness but does not assess treatment safety, longitudinal management, or patient outcomes
dataset is sourced from recent cases of the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) Clinical Pathological Conference (CPC), published as Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital
To run SDBench on the nejm dataset you will need to license the SDBench dataset from NEJM
